name: Charnia
fact: A frond-shaped organism discovered in Charnwood Forest, England by schoolboy Roger Mason in 1957 - the first Precambrian macrofossil recognized in the UK. Whether it was an alga, fungus, or early animal is still debated.
know: Charnia lived too deep for sunlight, so it cannot have been a plant. Growth series of fossils show it added new branches at its tip — a pattern seen in animals, not seaweeds.

name: Dickinsonia
size: A few mm to 1.4 m across
fact: A flat, ribbed oval like a quilted bath mat, with no mouth, gut or eyes that anyone can find. It grew by adding new segments at one end and seems to have fed by settling on the slimy microbial mat that carpeted the seafloor and digesting it from below.
know: For 70 years nobody could say whether Dickinsonia was an animal, a giant single cell, a lichen or a fungus. In 2018 chemists extracted fossil cholesterol from specimens in Russia's White Sea cliffs — a fat made by animals. It is among the oldest animals confirmed by chemistry.

name: Kimberella
fact: A slug-like creature with a soft, unmineralised shell and a frilled edge. It is the earliest fossil that most scientists accept as a bilaterian — an animal with a left and a right side, a front and a back, like us.
know: More than a thousand specimens are known, many lying next to fan-shaped scratch marks in the fossil microbial mat: the traces of an animal raking up food with a toothed, tongue-like organ, the way snails still do.

name: Fractofusus
fact: A spindle-shaped frond that lay flat on the deep seabed, built from branches that branch again, and again — the same pattern at every scale. It could not move, had no mouth, and absorbed nutrients straight from the water.
know: At Mistaken Point, Newfoundland, volcanic ash buried whole seafloor communities where they lived. Mapping thousands of Fractofusus showed small ones clustered around large ones — evidence they reproduced by sending out runners, like strawberry plants.

name: Spriggina
fact: A small, segmented animal with a crescent-shaped head — one of the first creatures with a definite front end. Named for Reg Sprigg, the geologist who found the Ediacara fossils in 1946 and was at first not believed.
debate: Is it a relative of arthropods, of segmented worms, or of nothing alive today? Its segments are slightly offset left and right, which no modern group does.

name: Tribrachidium
fact: A small disc with three spiral arms — threefold symmetry, a body plan no living animal uses. Computer models of water flowing over it suggest the arms steered food particles into pits on its surface: one of the oldest known suspension feeders.

name: Haootia
fact: An anchored, cup-shaped animal whose fossil preserves bundles of fibres arranged exactly like muscle. If so, it is the oldest evidence of muscle on Earth — and a likely relative of jellyfish and corals.

name: Cloudina
fact: A stack of tiny nested cones — one of the first animals to build a hard skeleton. Its tubes formed reefs with microbes, half a billion years before coral reefs.
know: Many Cloudina shells have neat round holes drilled into them. Something was boring through armour to eat the animal inside: the earliest sign of predators, and of the arms race that would explode in the Cambrian.

name: Doushantuo embryos
fact: Microscopic balls of 2, 4, 8, 16 cells and more, turned to phosphate so finely that individual cells — and in some, structures inside the cells — survive. They look like the earliest stages of an animal embryo.
debate: Animal embryos, or the dividing cysts of single-celled relatives of animals? X-ray scans can now see inside them cell by cell, and the argument continues.

name: Ikaria
size: About the size of a grain of rice
fact: A tiny worm-like animal with a front and back, a mouth and a gut — possibly close to the ancestor of almost every animal alive today, including us.
know: Scientists first found its burrows — tiny tunnels in fossil sand. In 2020, 3-D laser scans revealed the minute bodies that made them, right at the ends of the tunnels.

name: Rangea
fact: A frond built of repeating leaf-like units, each branching like a fern — one of the first Ediacaran fossils ever named, from Namibia, in 1929.

name: Funisia
fact: Clusters of tubes that grew from the seafloor in dense patches. Neighbouring tubes are always the same age.
know: Same-age clusters mean the young all settled at once — as happens when animals spawn. Funisia may be the oldest evidence of sexual reproduction in animals (2008).

name: Eoandromeda
fact: A dome with eight spiral arms, like a pinwheel. Found in both China and Australia.
debate: Its eight arms resemble the eight rows of paddles on a comb jelly — making it, perhaps, a very early relative of those animals. Others see no link at all.

name: Yorgia
fact: A flat, quilted oval. Behind some fossils lies a trail of faint body-shaped prints ending at the animal itself.
know: Each print marks a spot where it sat, digested the microbial mat beneath it, and then moved on — some of the oldest evidence of an animal moving under its own power.
